title: Foundations of Nursing Practice: Nutrition, Feeding & Aspiration Prevention
html:
Nutrition, hydration, and safe feeding help preserve recovery, function, comfort, and dignity. The RN assesses the person and the care plan together: what the client can safely consume, what support is needed, what has changed, and when the team must reassess. A meal tray or tube feeding is never routine when safety cues are present.

Learning goals

  • Recognize cues that increase risk during oral intake.
  • Use prescribed swallowing and diet precautions during feeding.
  • Assess nutrition and hydration patterns without assuming a diagnosis.
  • Apply ordered and policy-based safeguards for enteral feeding.
  • Escalate airway, breathing, and feeding-intolerance concerns promptly.

Recognize aspiration risk before feeding

Before providing oral intake, assess alertness, ability to sit safely, recent coughing or choking, wet or gurgly voice, shortness of breath, fatigue, neurologic change, dentition, and the current swallowing plan. Review the prescribed diet texture, fluid consistency, supervision level, and any speech-language pathology recommendations. A new concern is a reason to pause and seek the appropriate assessment; it is not a reason to test the client with water or independently liberalize the diet.

Pause for a safety cue
Coughing, throat clearing, voice change after swallowing, pocketing food, reduced alertness, or new respiratory symptoms may signal that the client needs reassessment before oral intake continues.

Silent aspiration: aspiration can occur without coughing or a wet voice. Absence of visible symptoms does not prove swallowing is safe; continue the individualized plan and obtain specialist reassessment when indicated.

Protect swallowing safety

Verify the client, diet order, and care plan. Provide food and fluids only in the ordered texture and consistency. When permitted by the plan and not contraindicated, support an awake client in an upright position and allow a slow pace with small bites or sips. Offer the amount and level of assistance specified in the plan; do not rush, force feed, or place food in the mouth of a drowsy client.

Stop oral intake if the client coughs repeatedly, chokes, develops a wet voice, cannot clear secretions, or develops new breathing difficulty. Keep the client safe, assess airway and breathing, and follow the escalation process. Sudden inability to speak, stridor, cyanosis, or acute respiratory distress requires immediate emergency response.

Assess nutrition and hydration, not just a tray

Ask about appetite, nausea, vomiting, pain, dietary preferences, cultural needs, food access, ability to self-feed, recent intake, and barriers to eating. Observe intake patterns, hydration clues, output when relevant, weight trends, energy, and tolerance of the plan. Record measurable information according to policy, such as the portion consumed or fluids taken. A single low-intake meal may require support and follow-up; a worsening pattern, new dysphagia concern, or dehydration cues merits communication with the appropriate team member.

Enteral feeding: follow the order and policy

For enteral feeding, trace the tubing from the client to the correct formula and verify the prescribed formula, route, rate, water flushes, and medication plan. Use the institution's approved placement-verification process before use and whenever a concern arises. An unexplained change in external tube length, new pain, vomiting, abdominal distention, coughing, or respiratory symptoms should prompt the RN to pause use as indicated by policy and obtain help. Do not advance the rate, change the formula, or use an unverified tube independently.

Keep the head of bed elevated to the degree specified by the care plan or policy; many adult protocols use 30–45 degrees unless contraindicated. This is a safeguard, not a substitute for ongoing assessment. Observe tolerance, protect skin at the tube site, provide oral care, and document the response and actions taken.

Evaluate nutrition and hydration outcomes

Evaluation considers more than whether food was offered. Reassess intake percentage, fluids, symptoms, respiratory status, ability to self-feed, weight trend when available, output, skin and oral status, and the client's goals or preferences. Communicate barriers and a plan that is not producing the expected response. The nursing process continues as the client's condition and ability change.

Clinical example

A client recovering from a stroke becomes drowsy at lunch and coughs after two bites of the ordered texture-modified meal. The RN stops the meal, keeps the client supported safely upright, assesses airway and breathing, reviews the swallowing plan, documents the objective cues, and obtains the required help. Continuing the tray to meet an intake goal would not be safe.
